_readme: Books and authors screened and excluded WITHOUT being read. One JSON object per line. Written by /book-screen; read by the viewer app. Read-and-disliked books are not here - they have a real score in books-read.md. The point of this file is that 'why isn't X in the list?' is answerable from data instead of from prose, and that the same ground is not screened twice.
_level: author | series | title | category - how wide the exclusion is. Scope matters: an Earthsea objection must not sink Le Guin, which is the false negative that produced the scoping rule.
_filter: The axis id that decided it, matching the ids in book-revs.json, or 'access' for an edition/availability problem. An access row is a dated fact and should be re-checked; an axis row is a judgement and only changes if that rule changes.
_backfill: Rows dated 2026-08-26 with a 'source' of authors-table or sweep-* were recovered from prose on 2026-08-26 when the viewer app was built. Before that they existed only as sentences in book-recommendations.md and in sweeps[].ruledOut.
_author: The author, omitted entirely for level=category where it does not apply. Do not write a placeholder like "(various)" - an absent field reads as absent, a placeholder reads as data.

author: Frank Herbert
why: Occult ritual enacted on the page. The messianic prominence is a separate, graded deduction and must not be cited as disqualifying.

author: Robert Jackson Bennett
why: Divinities are invented so the source test passes, but miracles are rituals learned and performed on the page by Shara and Sigrud - the depiction test, which is absolute. His Founders trilogy is unaffected and is a live candidate.

author: Ursula K. Le Guin
why: True-name spellcasting sits on the occult source test. Scoped to Earthsea only - her Hainish work passes and Leva ruka tmy is a live candidate. This row is why the scoping rule exists.

author: Steven Erikson
why: Many plot lines starting at once with no legible entry situation - the exact Guards! Guards! 30 failure.

author: Franz Kafka
why: Deliberately opaque and unfinished. Promena, also held, is not and is a live candidate.

author: George R. R. Martin
why: Heavy description with little story happening in it - the LOTR 84 sparseness penalty at far greater length. Content is also gratuitous rather than merely frequent, which is the costly kind.

author: Charles Bukowski
why: Crude sexual content is the whole register, which is the costly kind under the treatment rule - not the profanity, which costs nothing.

author: Philip Pullman
why: The reverence rule inverted: what costs is a treatment played for ridicule, which is the axis Narnia 67 passes on.

author: Varlam Salamov
why: Among the bleakest material in the catalogue. Bleakness is only a mild pushback, so this is a caution at the extreme end rather than a bar - listed here because it is the one place that axis alone decided it.

author: Ayaan Hirsi Ali
why: Argument rather than narrative - the no-apologetics-as-subject line. Rebelka (Infidel) is the live candidate instead. Same distinction recorded against Qureshi's other books.

author: Nabeel Qureshi
why: Highest non-fiction score in the log, but his other books are apologetics - theology as a subject in its own right.

author: C. S. Lewis
why: Excluded separately from Narnia 67, which was read and scored.

author: Slavomir Rawicz
why: The account is widely held to be fabricated, and real-world claims must be true - Ranger's Apprentice 74 was docked for exactly this. Do not propose without saying so.

author: Antoine de Saint-Exupery
why: Extends a Confirmed fit author but is posthumous and unfinished - the Unfinished Tales 69 failure mode. Kameny chramu is a curated selection from it and may dodge that.

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
why: The four read entries run 69-84 and the score tracks how finished and shaped the book is; the remaining volumes sit at the Unfinished Tales 69 end.

author: Douglas Adams
why: Read and scored 70 against book 1's 83 - the steepest series decline in the log. Listed so the app does not re-propose them.

author: Dmitry Glukhovsky
why: The only holding is the K. E. Macan audio edition for blind readers, not general-loan print. An access fact, so re-check it rather than treating it as a judgement.

why: Host 2025 record has an empty responsibility statement, so the author cannot be confirmed from the catalogue. Verify before proposing.

entity: Anglophone crime, detective and procedural fiction
why: The hard mystery filter, applied once at category level so heading sweeps stop re-surfacing it. Covers the bulk of the unconsidered anglicka/americka proza shelf: Cornwell is not here but May 24 titles, Bryndza 19, Marsons 18, Granger 17, Grisham 17, Weaver 13, Deaver 13, Connelly 12, Patterson 12+12, Castillo 14, Gibney 11, Penny 10, Tremayne 10, Stabenow 11, Berry 10, Robb 17. Individual rows for these would cost ~230 lines and remove nothing else.

Covers Steel 30, Cartland 23, Howell 16, Yarros 16, Moyes 16, Riley 16, Maas 15, Quinn 14, Caplin 14, Hoover 12, Perry 12, Probst 11, James 10, Huang 10, Moreland 10, Armentrout 10, Kinsella 10, Sparks 10. Register alone would NOT justify this; the sexual content being the point of the book is what does.

Wrong audience rather than a taste objection - not the graded child-protagonist pushback, which applies to adult books with child leads (Ender 87, Little Prince 82). Covers Walliams 29, Wilson 19, Dahl's children's titles, Stevens 10, Webb 10, Horacek 11. NOTE: Dahl's ADULT short fiction (Tales of the Unexpected) is not covered by this row and is a live lead.

Hard mystery filter, recorded once at category level. This is the single largest block on the ceska proza shelf: Vondruska 54 titles (Oldrich z Chlumu medieval investigations), Ceska 36, Bauer 34 (his historical-mystery output), Harasimova 16, Niedl 15, Klevisova 10, Brezina 10, Josef Klima 9. Per-author rows would cost ~180 lines and remove nothing else.

Wrong audience, not the graded child-protagonist pushback that applies to adult books with child leads (Ender 87, Little Prince 82). Covers Pospisilova 38, Brezinova 34, Krolupperova 32, Peroutkova 19, Braunova 17, Roznovska 14, Valkova 12, Brezina/Brezina 24, Drijverova 10, Ctvrtek 10, Fisarova 9, Kratochvil 9. IMPORTANT: it also covers most of Stancik's 23 records (Jezevec Chrujda, H2O) and most of Pilatova's 27 (animal picture books) - their raw counts made them look like major literary finds and they are not.

entity: Czech commercial sentimental fiction (Ikar / Motto / Cosmopolis / Alpress / MOBA women's-fiction lines)
why: DEPRIORITISED, NOT HARD-FILTERED - recorded so the distinction is explicit. Jakoubkova 26, Whitton 24, Kornerova 10, Vanova 9, Mlynarova 9 and the bulk of ~1400 Ikar/Motto/Cosmopolis/Alpress/MOBA records. These are sentimental rather than crude, so axis:sexual-treatment does NOT apply and rejecting them under it would have been wrong. The objection is a low ideas ceiling, which is a GRADED axis: the profile forbids silently excluding on graded axes. Treat this row as a search-priority hint, not a verdict, and re-open any specific title the reader asks about.

author: Neil Gaiman
why: Real-world pantheons as literal characters with worship and sacrifice enacted on the page - the occult source AND depiction tests. Scoped to this title: Kniha hrbitova and Krehke veci are not covered and remain unassessed. Recorded as data 2026-08-26 after the first full model run scored it 5; the ruling had existed only as prose in a sweeps[].ruledOut block, so no join could see it.

author: Terry Pratchett a Neil Gaiman
why: Two independent hits. The opening is the Discworld failure mode at higher density - Eden, Crowley and Aziraphale, the baby swap, the Them, Anathema, Newt and the Horsemen all start inside the first sixty pages, and Discworld was tried twice and scored 30 on exactly this. Second, Christian eschatology is played for comedy throughout; the graded prophecy axis is about reverence rather than resemblance, and a treatment played for ridicule is the one case the profile names as not fine. Scoped to this title. It does NOT extend to Gaiman, whose Kniha hrbitova and Krehke veci remain unassessed, and it does not widen the existing Discworld row.

entity: Hrbitov zapomenutych knih (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books)
author: Carlos Ruiz Zafón
why: Covers both score-5 rows, Stin vetru and Labyrint duchu. The series engine is investigation: who Julian Carax was and who is burning his books in volume 1, and by volume 4 the viewpoint character Alicia Gris is a police investigator working a case. The reader hard-filters detective and mystery, and here the mystery is not a subplot but the reason to keep reading. Stated confidence: medium-high. This is literary Gothic rather than crime fiction, so if the filter is meant narrowly - whodunits only - Stin vetru is the row to revisit first, on its atmosphere and its Barcelona.

author: John Steinbeck
why: Joseph Wayne's worship of a rock and glade is not metaphor in this book; he makes offerings to it and the novel ends with a blood sacrifice performed to bring rain, presented as efficacious. That is prayer and sacrifice to a real-world deity enacted on the page, which the filter names explicitly, and it is the subject rather than an incident. Scoped to this title - Steinbeck is otherwise unassessed and nothing here touches Of Mice and Men or The Grapes of Wrath.

author: Bernard Cornwell
why: The sword-consecration 'pit slaughter' scene: a man, a horse, a ram, a bull and a drake sacrificed to Odin, plus a smith's spell and a woman's separate night-rite over the blade, all narrated as it happens, not mentioned as a past event.

author: Samantha Shannon
why: A first-person dreamwalker narrator who acts by leaving her body to possess other minds, surrounded by working necromancers, binders, exorcists, summoners, mediums and card-and-bone diviners carried under those real occult disciplines' own names. Enacted on the page throughout, and the book's central conflict is a regime hunting exactly this practice.

author: Samantha Shannon
why: The narrator's defining and constantly used ability is to leave her body and possess another person's body or dreamscape, performed on the page; the Paris clairvoyant underworld she operates in runs on card divination, scrying, blood-and-bone reading, spirit summoning, binding and necromancy, all real occult disciplines carried under their own names rather than an invented system.

author: Samantha Shannon
why: Tarot cartomancy read aloud for the protagonist in a scene, mediums bodily possessed by spirits of the dead who then paint through them, and an order of clairvoyants who summon, bind, exorcise and raise the dead. The taxonomy is lifted from real divination disciplines under their own names, so it is not an invented system, and the practices are enacted on the page.

author: Isaac Asimov
why: An explicit science-fiction whodunit. Baley is called to Solaria to solve the murder of Rikaine Delmarre, the plot runs as interrogation through a fixed suspect list, and the resolution is the identification of the murderer through a loophole in the wording of the Three Laws. Sources describe the book as a whodunit in the same mould as its predecessor.

author: Jane Harperova
why: Crime novel built on two investigations - the Hadler murder-suicide and Ellie Deacon's drowning twenty years earlier - carried by AFP investigator Aaron Falk together with the local police sergeant. Won the CWA Gold Dagger for Best Crime Novel and the British Book Awards Crime and Thriller Book of the Year.

author: Samantha Shannon
why: The protagonist detaches her spirit and possesses another person's body on the page to win the syndicate's scrimmage, and tracks an enemy along an ectoplasm-activated spirit bond. Shannon's own Waterstones piece on this setting describes augurs reading human and animal innards, blood and tears to reach the spirit world. Real occult disciplines, enacted in scene.

author: Sabaa Tahir
why: Divination enacted on the page. In a Lahore flashback chapter in Part One, Misbah is taken by her cousin to a fortune teller in Anarkali Bazaar who reads her palms and predicts a restless-souled husband, a voyage across the sea and three children, then says 'You will fail them all'; Misbah offers money to have the fortune changed and is refused. Three independent chapter summaries place the scene in Part One and agree the novel is structured around the prophecy coming true. Palmistry is a real-world occult practice and it is performed in a scene, so both the source and the depiction test fail.

author: Jane Harperova
why: Missing-person investigation led by AFP investigator Aaron Falk with Sergeant Raco, plus a second suspicious death at the same location. Won the 2023 Ned Kelly Award for Best Novel, an Australian crime-fiction prize, and is reviewed throughout as mystery/crime fiction.

author: Ben Kane
why: Etruscan haruspicy performed on the page in chapter one: Olenus reads the buzzards over the temple of Tinia and declares the omens bad, and the apprentice is being taught liver and entrail divination. Real-world divination, enacted in a scene, and the foretelling is presented as genuinely working.

author: Neil Gaiman
why: A ritual with candles and herbs is performed on the page to send the protagonist to the Beginning of the World, repeated later via seance; an earlier spell split him in two; and he petitions and bargains with real folkloric deities. Source and depiction tests both fail, with no mechanical account.

author: Julian Barnes
why: Mediumship and seances are practised on the page, not merely referred to: Doyle is written as a convinced spiritualist in the last third, and the final section stages the Albert Hall attempt to contact him after his death, with the medium in trance and the dead speaking through her. Real-world occult source, enacted depiction, no mechanical account.

author: Laini Taylor
why: Soul-gleaning into thuribles on incense smoke and body-making from strings of human teeth - necromancy under the Source test - carried out on the page, with pain and secrecy as the mechanism rather than declared rules.

author: Laini Taylor
why: The protagonist performs the resurrection rite on the page throughout - souls gleaned into thuribles, bodies made from human teeth, powered by a pain tithe - which is necromancy in source and a rite in depiction, with no mechanical account of it.

author: Miloš Urban
why: Pagan rites are enacted on the page, not mentioned as past practice: animal sacrifice offered to keep the pagan gods favourable in the first book, a rocking stone established as a ritual site and place of sacrifice in the prologue, the narrative segmented by a cycle of folk-magical feasts including Walpurgis night, and a human sacrifice performed in the closing scene. Drawn from real Czech folk religion, with no mechanical account of any of it.

author: Neil Gaiman
why: Tea-leaf divination is performed on the page in chapter 2 and is plot-functional - it yields the warning and the hag stone, a real-folklore protective amulet later used to see the dead children's souls. Divination is named on the source list, the depiction is enacted rather than reported, and no mechanical account is offered.

author: William Gibson
why: A murder witnessed early, an investigator assembling the case, and a protagonist whose function is to identify the killer - reviewers call it a basic whodunnit with a witness to protect.

author: Robert Galbraith
why: A cold-case whodunnit and the fifth of a detective series: Strike and Ellacott reconstruct a forty-year-old disappearance from unreliable witnesses, and the reviews agree the payoff is the construction of the mystery and its denouement rather than anything else.

author: Neil Gaiman
why: An angel is the central power the quest serves and bargains with; a rat-worship cult acts on its god's command on the page; the Black Friars administer a ritual ordeal; a resurrection runs on the externalised-soul motif from real folklore. Sources state the magic is deliberately unsystematised, so the mechanical-account escape is unavailable.

author: Siri Pettersen
why: A worshipped Seer, a Council and an order of assassins acting in His name, stone circles as portals, and a blessing rite conferring the Seer's protection that the plot turns on - devotion and invocation with no mechanical account of the Might that is bound on the page.

author: Siri Pettersen
why: The world's power is bound by characters on the page with no mechanical account, inside a theocracy of a worshipped Seer, a priest-like Council, devotional rites and stone-circle portals - devotion and invocation, not declared rules.

author: H. P. Lovecraft
why: Necromancy drawn from actual occultism and performed on the page: a two-hour chanted invocation using real divine names calls a dead man back from his ashes, with resurrection and dissolution formulae invoking a named deity, and no mechanical account of the practice.

author: Otfried Preussler
why: Fails both occult tests at once and at the centre of the book. Twelve apprentices in a Sorbian water-mill are taught black magic from the Master's Koraktor - the source is documented Lusatian sorcery lore, not an invented system - and the instruction, the transformations and the yearly blood-price are performed on the page as the plot's working mechanism. There is no mechanical account of any of it. This is the configuration the 2026-08-26 ruling made a veto.

author: Otfried Preussler
why: A witch practising witchcraft on the page as the entire premise - spells cast from a spell book, broom flight, a witches' sabbath on Walpurgis Night. Source test fails on real-folklore witchcraft, depiction test fails on rites enacted. Scoped to this title and to Čarodějův učeň; nothing here touches Preussler's Loupežník Zuřivous, which is a robber farce.

author: Eiko Kadono
why: The protagonist is a witch serving her apprenticeship year: broom flight and spellwork are what she does in scene after scene. Gentle in tone, which is not the axis - the axis is whether witchcraft in the historical mould is practised on the page, and it is. Same reason Harry Potter 51 and Percy Jackson 57 sit where they do.

author: Diana Wynne Jones
why: Wizards and witches casting spells and curses on the page, plus Howl's contract with a fire demon, in a system that is invented but is explicitly spellcasting in the historical-occult mould with no mechanical account of how it works. That is the exact cell the 2026-08-26 ruling closed against Jonathan Strange. Medium-high confidence; scoped to this title, so the rest of Wynne Jones is unassessed rather than rejected.

entity: Zlobryně a sirotci (The Girl Who Drank the Moon)
author: Kelly Barnhill
why: A witch who draws magic out of moonlight and enmagicks a child, with the drawing and the spellwork done on the page. The magic is invented, so the source test passes, but the depiction test fails and there is no engineering-style account of the mechanism. Confidence medium - the reading is from reviews and plot summaries, not the text - so this is the likeliest row in this screen to be worth revisiting if the reader disagrees.

author: Jean-Claude Mourlevat
why: Catalogued by the library itself as detektivní příběhy: a murder, a wrongly suspected protagonist and an investigation are the whole engine of both held volumes (Jefferson dělá, co může, Jefferson se zlobí, Baobab 2023 and 2025). Hard mystery filter. Scoped to this series only - Mourlevat's Zimní bitva is recorded as a candidate and is untouched by this row.

author: Erich Kästner
why: The plot is an investigation from the second chapter on: Emil is robbed on a train and a gang of Berlin boys tails, traps and identifies the thief, ending in a police station. Stated confidence medium - it is a children's chase story rather than crime fiction, so if the mystery filter is meant narrowly this is the first row in this screen to revisit. Scoped to this title; Kästner's other work is unassessed.

DEPRIORITISED, NOT HARD-FILTERED, and recorded so the next children's sweep does not re-read the same 1,000 names. The literatura pro děti a mládež heading is dominated by age-banded serials written to a formula and a length: Brezina 32 titles, Hunter (Warriors) 26, Stewner 20, Kinney 19, Cobb 18, Peroutková 17, Březinová 15, Webb 14, Válková 13, Pospíšilová 13, Chapman 11, Small 11, Cowell 10, Griffiths 10, Pantermüller 10, Štulcová 10, Kopecká 10, plus a long tail of 1-4-title authors in the same mould. Wrong audience rather than a taste objection - the axis:childrens deduction here is total, not graded, because there is no adult layer for it to grade.

Minecraft, Disney, Five Nights at Freddy's and football-star tie-ins: Cube Kid 8, Morgan Winter 4, Frigiel, Books Kid, Plays Stacy, Cawthon 3, Behling 2, Marsoli 2, Parent, Hutta, Mugford 9, Oldfield. Work-for-hire novelisation of a licensed property, so there is no authored premise for any axis to engage. Recorded at category level once; the keyword 'Minecraft' alone tags 59 records.

author: Julian Barnes
why: Paul, 19, is paired with the 48-year-old married Susan at a suburban tennis club, they begin an affair, and he then takes her away from her abusive husband to London, where the rest of the novel follows her decline into alcoholism and his life afterwards. Susan cannot bring herself to tell a solicitor why she wants a divorce, so she stays married to Gordon and the relationship stays an affair for its whole duration. This is not one thread among several - it is the only story the book has, so remove the infidelity and there is no novel, which is premise level whatever the framing. Marriage: Susan Macleod is married to Gordon Macleod and is the mother of two nearly grown daughters; she never divorces him, so her whole relationship with nineteen-year-old Paul Roberts is adulterous from start to finish

author: Francis Scott Fitzgerald
why: Nick Carraway narrates the summer Gatsby throws parties to win back Daisy Buchanan, who married Tom while Gatsby was away at war. The book runs on two adulteries at once - Gatsby's pursuit of a married woman, resumed with Nick's help, and Tom's open affair with the married Myrtle - and they produce the climax directly: Myrtle runs into the road for Tom's car, Daisy kills her, George kills Gatsby. Take the infidelity out and nothing of the plot survives, so it is the premise, and Fitzgerald's contempt for the Buchanans does not change the verdict. Marriage: Daisy is married to Tom Buchanan and Gatsby's entire project is to take her from him; in parallel Tom keeps Myrtle Wilson, married to George Wilson, in a Manhattan flat rented for the affair

author: W. Somerset Maughham
why: In colonial Hong Kong the vain Kitty, who married Walter at twenty-five without loving him, conducts an affair with the married Charles Townsend; Walter catches them and gives her the choice of a court case or accompanying him into a cholera epidemic inland, where the work at the convent remakes her. Every event in the book is caused by the adultery - the discovery, the ultimatum, the journey, the pregnancy of uncertain paternity, Walter's death - and she falls back into bed with Townsend even after all of it. Remove the infidelity and there is no plot, so this is premise level and Maugham's severe moral verdict on her does not change the outcome. Marriage: Kitty Fane is married to the bacteriologist Walter Fane and takes as her lover Charles Townsend, the Assistant Colonial Secretary, who is himself married to Dorothy Townsend - two marriages, one affair

author: John Fowles
why: Victorian Lyme Regis, 1867: a gentleman engaged to a pretty conventional heiress becomes obsessed with the disgraced Sarah Woodruff, meets her clandestinely, is seduced by her in an Exeter hotel and is ruined by breaking his engagement, all of it framed by a modern narrator who offers alternative endings. The betrayal of an in-scope bond is the entire plot and the whole reader experience is spent inside the triangle - the postmodern apparatus is commentary on that story, not a substitute for it. That is premise level, so it rejects regardless of the Victorian machinery that punishes Charles for it. Marriage: Charles Smithson is engaged to Ernestina Freeman, a wealthy merchant's daughter, throughout the book, and courts her while meeting Sarah Woodruff in secret; in the branch Fowles treats as real he sleeps with Sarah and then breaks the engagement, and Ernestina's father extracts a written confession that he acted dishonourably. Engagement is inside the scope of this gate.

author: Michel Faber
why: Victorian London, 1870s: the heir to a perfume business takes a brothel prostitute as his kept woman, funds her, and finally moves her into his own household while his wife sinks into madness. Every summary describes the book as two women, wife Agnes and mistress Sugar, revolving around the married William Rackham. The adulterous triangle is the central relationship and the engine of the conflict, not one thread among many, so it is premise level whatever the Victorian-prostitution framing. Marriage: William Rackham is married to Agnes; Sugar, a nineteen-year-old prostitute, becomes his exclusive kept mistress and is then installed in the marital house as governess to their daughter

author: Sandra Gulland
why: A historical novel of Louise de la Valliere, the horse-taming minor noblewoman who became the first maitresse en titre of the married Louis XIV, bore him four children and was then supplanted by Montespan. The whole arc is the secret affair, its exposure, her conscience and her fall. Remove the adultery with a married king and nothing of the book remains, so it is premise level despite the weak lexicon tier. Marriage: Louis XIV is married to Queen Marie-Therese of Spain; Louise de la Valliere is his mistress, later displaced by her friend Madame de Montespan

author: Jojo Moyesová
why: 1960: a socialite wakes from a car crash with amnesia and reconstructs, from hidden love letters, the affair she was having behind her cold husband's back; a 2003 journalist finds the same letters and reunites the pair after forty years. The adulterous correspondence is the title, the structure and the whole plot of both timelines. That is premise level, and the framing is openly romantic, but framing does not enter the veto. Marriage: Jennifer Stirling is married to the industrialist Laurence Stirling; her lover is the journalist Anthony O'Hare, whom she plans to leave her husband for

author: Joann Sfar
why: Not a new work: the Albatros 2009 comic adaptation of Le Petit Prince, which the reader has already read and scored 82. It reached a score of 5 in the crossover ranking only because the record's author field is the adapter, so the already-read join could not see it. Wrong format as well as a duplicate.

author: Martin Baltscheit
why: A licensed franchise spin-off, not Saint-Exupery: the Little Prince returns to Earth at Christmas, meets Jezisek and reflects on the meaning of the holiday (CPress 2020). Scored 5 by the ranking model, which was scoring the brand - the clearest single case of canonicity bleed the pass produced, and worth recording as the mechanism rather than just the title.

author: Naomi Novik
why: Ve stinu Hvozdu and V zajeti zimy both run on Slavic-folklore witchcraft cast on the page, which fails the occult source test. This ruling had existed since 2026-08-26 but ONLY as prose in the Authors table of book-recommendations.md, so no join could read it - the v4 corpus run scored her Letni valka (Host 2026) a 5 as a result. Recorded as a row now. Scoped to the author; a future Novik with no witchcraft would need its own pass.

author: Philip K. Dick
why: I Ching divination (a real-world practice) is consulted on-page repeatedly by multiple characters as a genuine plot-driving oracle, including a scene where an I-Ching-infused artifact grants a mystical vision - a rite enacted on page from a real occult source, not a declared mechanism.

author: Erin Morgenstern
why: A rite (a blood ritual: cutting the fingertips as an initiation, then healing them) is enacted on the page as part of magical training, and the system is explicitly ruleless/opaque (ancient texts, hereditary gift, binding pacts) rather than a declared mechanism, so it fails both the source and depiction tests.

author: Jean Rhys
why: Christophine's obeah love potion in Part Two is drawn from a real Caribbean folk-magic tradition (spellcasting), not an invented system, and the novel depicts it as genuinely effective on Rochester rather than as superstition - fails the occult filter's Source test.

author: Kristyna Snegonova
why: Priests/priestesses of an invented pantheon (death-god 'the Rider', goddess of life) perform temple duties and prayer on the page. Per the ruling this fails the depiction test regardless of the pantheon being invented, since it involves priesthood, invocation and devotion rather than a mechanical, engineered system.

author: Michael Scott
why: Elemental magic and aura-work are taught and used on the page, and the source material for one twin's power is explicitly the Witch of Endor, a real biblical necromancer - real-world-mould magic actually practised, not an invented mechanical system.

author: Eve Makis
why: Grandmother's coffee-ground divination is performed repeatedly on the page and her predictions are shown to genuinely come true, central to the plot -- real-world tasseography fails both the source and depiction tests.

author: Vladimir Sorokin
why: Protagonist visits a clairvoyant who performs a fire-based divination rite (burning books to read prophecy) on the page; real-world-style divination fails the occult source test outright.

author: Chaim Potok

author: Kristyna Freiova

author: Vilma Kadleckova
why: An alien priesthood performs on-page liturgical rites (a robed priest, a sacred object, prescribed ritual gestures at an altar) and a mourning ritual that requires human sacrifice of survivors, which the Church refuses to forgo. A rite enacted on the page vetoes even an invented religion.

author: Choderlos de Laclos
why: The novel's two seduction plots are both infidelity within scope - a married woman's affair and an engaged woman's corruption - and are the entire engine of the book; premise-level, so a reject regardless of the tragic framing.

author: Tahereh Mafi
why: Cosmology and the devil figure (Iblees/Iblis/Shaytan) are drawn directly from real Islamic religious tradition rather than invented, and the devil appears to and speaks with the protagonist on the page.

author: Jakub Hoza
why: An invented goddess with an active priesthood performing devotions (a priest receiving visions through prayer as a driving plot thread) - the ladder's own stated example of a veto despite an invented deity.

author: Hayley Hoskins
why: The twins' business is holding regular seance sessions where clients hear from dead relatives through them - literal mediumship/seance, named explicitly in the source-test veto list, enacted on page as an ongoing practice rather than a mentioned past event; no mechanical framing rescues it.

author: Lynn Flewelling
why: On-page spirit-binding/unbinding rite (bone doll, bone cut from the protagonist's own chest, white fire) built on a necromancy-mould magic system explicitly tied to a 'nation of necromancers.'

author: Joy Fieldingová
why: The book is structured around a shooting investigation with a whodunit reveal; reviewers praise the seeded clues and the final twist as its signature feature.

author: Zdenek Rehak
why: The book is a sci-fi detective novel built entirely around a detective's investigation into a missing person that turns into a murder case; the reader's satisfaction is explicitly whodunnit.

author: Andrzej Sapkowski
why: The saga's magic is sorceress/witchcraft-mould (invocation, magic amulets, blood prophecy) with no mechanical account, and books-read.md's own Witcher entry states this directly caused the occult filter to fire on the same saga ('The magic is the occult filter').

author: Rick Mofina
why: Central engine is a police investigation into a missing child with the family as suspects, resolved by a mystery-reveal twist - the reader's satisfaction is finding out what happened, the detective/mystery filter.

author: František Kotleta
why: Lucifer and Lilith, drawn directly from real Judeo-Christian demonology, are the book's active supernatural framework, not an invented system.

author: Tahereh Mafi
why: Continues the same Jinn/Iblees cosmology drawn from real Islamic religious tradition established in the first volume, with the devil figure still actively steering events.

author: Madeline Miller
why: The gods of the actual Greek pantheon act directly on the page - Thetis, Zeus, the Fates - and the plot turns on a real historical-religion rite: Iphigenia is sacrificed to appease the goddess Artemis so the fleet can sail, staged and witnessed on the page, with Achilles horrified by his own role in it. This is the same test that already cost Percy Jackson in this reader's own log ('the Greek pantheon counts, not just witchcraft') - a source drawn from actual historical religion, with a rite enacted rather than merely mentioned, fails both halves of the occult test.

author: Bernard Cornwell
why: Iseult is a sorceress whose prophetic power is treated as real in-world and is shown performing a divination for Uhtred on the page; the source (Celtic seer-folklore, 'shadow queens') is real-world-styled, not an invented or mechanical system, so it fails both tests the filter sets out.

author: Maggie Stiefvaterová
why: Tarot readings and an annual graveyard divination rite to see the spirits of the soon-to-be-dead are performed on the page by Blue's psychic family - real-world-sourced divination, enacted rather than merely mentioned, with no mechanical framing.

author: Jean Kwoková
why: The book's central and marketed satisfaction is a multi-POV investigation into what happened to a missing family member, including a suspected-murder red herring before the reveal - the whodunit shape the filter targets, even though the eventual cause is suicide rather than murder.

author: Emily Itami
why: Married protagonist's affair with Kiyoshi is the entire engine of the plot - premise level, always a reject regardless of the non-judgmental framing.

author: Faridah Àbíké-Íyímídé
why: The plot's central engine and marketed hook is identifying the anonymous blackmailer 'Aces' - a whodunnit structure.

author: Rachel Caine
why: The book's central engine is Gwen investigating a missing-person cold case, uncovering new suspects and victims as she gets closer to the truth - the reader's satisfaction is finding out what happened, the definition of the detective/mystery filter.

author: J.R. Ward
why: Each Black Dagger Brotherhood book's plot is a single new couple's courtship; here Axe and Elise's developing sexual relationship is the book, not a thread in a larger plot. Reviews confirm explicit, steamy content beyond the reviewers' own usual PG-13 ceiling, with a 'bonding scene' singled out as the standout. Remove the sexual relationship and there is no book - the same premise test used elsewhere in the ladder.

author: Kristin Harmel
why: Two marital affairs (Ines and the Nazi-collaborator Antoine; Michel and Celine) are the engine of the book's central crisis - a murder's exposure, a sexual assault, and a fatal betrayal to the authorities all flow directly from them. Remove the affairs and the wartime plot has no engine left; this is premise level, not backstory or subplot.

author: Robert Low
why: Real Norse pagan sacrifice and worship rites are enacted on the page across the series (women sacrificed in pagan tombs, 'fervent rituals' to the Old Gods, prayer to real Norse deities) - both the source and depiction tests of the occult filter fail.

author: Alison Goodman
why: The Dragoneye magic is explicitly built on real-world East Asian astrology and spirituality, not an invented system: the twelve energy dragons are modeled on the Chinese zodiac, and feng shui and tai chi meditation are the actual described mechanics of how power is drawn (life-force called 'hua'). That fails the Source test. It also fails Depiction: the book's central set piece is a formal ceremony in which an ascendant dragon spirit chooses and bonds with a human apprentice on the page - candidates feel the dragon's spirit 'ripple through' them during the rite itself, not merely hear that it happened. Nothing in the system is described as declared rules operating like technology; it is devotional and ceremonial throughout, so the mechanism escape does not apply.

author: Alison Goodman
why: The duology's magic is built directly on real-world East Asian astrological and spiritual practice, not an invented system: Goodman models the twelve energy dragons on the Chinese zodiac and layers in feng shui and tai chi meditation as the actual mechanics of how a Dragoneye draws power (draining life-force called 'hua'). That fails the Source test on its own. It also fails Depiction: the selection where a dragon spirit chooses and bonds with its apprentice is staged as a formal on-page ritual ('a day of great ritual and ceremony') that the candidate feels 'ripple through his blood' - a rite enacted on the page, not merely referenced as having happened. There is no mechanical/engineering account of the power (no declared technological rules, only devotion, ceremony and zodiac correspondence), so the mechanism escape does not apply. Eona continues the same bonded Mirror Dragon power established in Eon, so the same veto applies to both books in the duology.

author: Terry Pratchett
why: Discworld's witches fail the occult filter on BOTH tests, which is a veto on either alone. Source: they are drawn from documented English and European folk witchcraft rather than invented - covens, a cauldron, broomstick flight, a Midsummer rite at a stone circle, and in one volume a practitioner of real-world Vodou. Depiction: the rites are performed on the page as the story's working mechanism, and the 2026-08-26 ruling settled that a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented. This is exactly the Harry Potter 51 objection in the reader's own words - invented magic as fantasy worldbuilding is fine, magic drawn from real-world historical witchcraft is not - and occult is the most severe objection in the log, with the three books that fail it sitting at 51, 53 and 57. Scoped to the witches strand only: Mort 83 is a Discworld novel with a spell-casting wizard in it and drew no objection, so this is not a verdict on the setting or the author.

author: Eoin Colfer
why: Control runes branded onto a person, an enslaving curse laid on two leads, and a crowd mesmerised - all enacted on the page, with no mechanical account of the system; the series' fairy magic is separately replenished by a rite performed under a full moon.

author: Francoise Sagan
why: Infidelity within a marriage is the premise: the whole novel is the married Ludovic's affair with his mother-in-law Fanny, with his father as a third corner of the triangle. The Spectator's review describes the book as 'three sides of a love triangle composed of a son, a father, and a mother-in-law'; publisher and review copy agree Fanny arrives intending to patch up her daughter's marriage and instead takes the husband. Remove the affair and there is no book.

author: Anne O’Brienová
why: Infidelity is the premise. Edward III is married to Philippa for the span of the relationship the whole novel consists of, and the book is the mistress's life, rise and downfall on that footing; remove it and no book remains. Framing is irrelevant to the test.

author: Philippa Gregory
why: Infidelity is the premise: a married man's affair with the queen is the whole plot, his wife is one of the narrating points of view, and the catalogue's own annotation states it in one line - 'though married, he meets there the love of his life'. Marriage scope satisfied; framing is irrelevant to the premise test.

author: Tanja Heitmann
why: Demonic possession, blood sacrifices made to a demon by the protagonist, and sacrificial rites as the central plot business. Fails Source (real-world occult material) and Depiction (rites enacted, not reported), with no mechanical account of any of it.

author: Kate Furnivallová
why: The premise is an affair conducted during a formal betrothal: the heroine is engaged to a count her parents chose while carrying on with the Danish engineer the book is marketed as being about. Remove it and there is no book; engagement is inside the filter's scope.

author: Petr Mandík
why: Witches and witchcraft in the real-world mould, not an invented system: a reform school for witches, a heroine who discovers her witch powers and is taught to use them, and magic used on the page with no mechanical account of how it works.

author: Simon Sebag Montefiore
why: Adultery inside a marriage is the premise of the book's main action. Sashenka is married to Vanya Palitsyn; the publisher's description of Part Two frames the forbidden affair with Benya Golden as what 'will have devastating consequences', and Publishers Weekly states that her affair with a disgraced writer leads directly to the arrests, the torture and the choice between her family, her lover and her cause - the event the 1994 frame narrative is built to uncover.

author: Thomas C. Brezina
why: The series is published as a Rate-Krimi (puzzle-crime) for young readers: the three leads solve the case 'gemeinsam mit dem Leser', the volumes ship with a detective kit, and the picture puzzles exist so the reader can catch a suspect lying. Detective/mystery is a hard filter.

author: Kendare Blake
why: The Fennbirn Goddess with a priesthood and claiming rites, and a whole novella built on the oracle queen's gift of sight - divination as the subject, not as a past event. Source and Depiction both fail with no mechanical account.

author: TJ Klune
why: A Ouija-board seance conducted on the page, with the dead protagonist working the planchette and answering the medium - the occult apparatus is shown functioning, not debunked - inside an afterlife framework of reapers, a ferryman and Charon's Crossing with no mechanical account.

author: Robert Low
why: Real Norse paganism, enacted not recalled. The crew's defining act is a spoken oath to Odin, which the narrator takes on joining them and which reviewers identify as the book's structural spine; a reviewer also records the narrator witnessing a human sacrifice on the page. Real deity, real historical rite, no mechanical account.

author: Kristen Britain
why: Necromancy in the real-world occult mould, enacted on the page: soul-ensnaring arrows, a bound ghost of the dead messenger accompanying the heroine, an on-page possession from which she retains the dead man's skill, magicians sacrificing their lives to raise a warding wall, and an enemy who made his spirit immortal by dark magic. The magic is innate talent triggered by a brooch, with no declared mechanical account, so the engineering exemption does not apply.

author: Kendare Blake
why: Goddess-worship with a priesthood and a High Priestess, human sacrifice treated as efficacious, a divinatory sight gift, and blood-cost low magic performed on the page to bind a familiar. Source and Depiction both fail and there is no mechanical account.

author: Anthony Horowitz
why: The setting is explicitly a school of black magic training wizards and witches in the dark arts - real-world witchcraft in source - and the practice is enacted on the page: signing the register in blood, black rings worn by every pupil, a master transforming at the full moon, and a contest for the Unholy Grail. No mechanical account of the system is offered.
